name: Review of Case-Based Reasoning for LLM Agents: Theoretical Foundations, Architectural Components, and Cognitive Integration (Hatalis et al.)

code_url: N/A (this is a theoretical/conceptual review with no original experiments; the authors release no code or implementation repository. GitHub/framework references in the text are citations to third-party CBR-LLM systems such as DS-Agent, CaseGPT, and CBR-RAG, not an artifact of this paper.)
maintained_repo_url: N/A (no continuously-updated authors' paper list or leaderboard repository; the work is a frozen arXiv PDF, last revised to v2 on 11 Apr 2025).
task_domain: Survey / review (decision-making and agent reasoning). Reviews how Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) can be integrated into LLM-agent frameworks for planning, structured/specialized-knowledge tasks, and accountable decision-making. Surveyed application domains of the cited CBR-LLM systems span automated data science (DS-Agent), healthcare and legal QA (CaseGPT, CBR-RAG), triage classification, logical fallacy detection, code generation, and multiagent gaming/goal reasoning, rather than a single task domain.
problem_setting: Analytical literature review plus a proposed theoretical/mathematical framework -- not a method with original experiments. It (1) reviews the theoretical foundations of CBR-augmented LLM agents, (2) identifies critical architectural components, (3) formulates a mathematical model of the CBR processes of case retrieval, adaptation, and learning (mapping the classic Aamodt & Plaza 4R cycle Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain onto LLM agents), (4) gives a qualitative comparative analysis of CBR-LLM vs Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning vs vanilla RAG, and (5) explores cognitive dimensions (self-reflection, introspection, curiosity) integrated with Goal-Driven Autonomy (GDA). It covers both single-agent and multi-agent (multiagent gaming GDA) settings and interactive/online learning settings as surveyed sub-areas, but defines no controlled experimental protocol or benchmark of its own; all quantitative numbers are drawn from cited works.
what_is_retrieved: Cases (problem-solution-outcome episodes). In the proposed framework a case is the unit; surveyed CBR-LLM systems retrieve past cases / problem-solution pairs / exemplars / nearest-neighbor precedent cases (e.g., DS-Agent retrieves expert case insights; Dannenhauer et al. retrieve NL-task/Python-code problem-solution pairs; CBR-RAG retrieves contextually relevant legal cases).
retrieval_grounding: HYBRID / GROWING (episodic) memory. The defining framing is a GROWING agent-owned case library L that the agent writes to via the Retain phase (L_{t+1} = L_t U {c_new} when utility >= delta), as opposed to a static external corpus. CBR is explicitly contrasted with vanilla RAG's reference-based corpus retrieval; the case library evolves over time, making it a growing/episodic store (HYBRID where seeded from an offline expert case base as in DS-Agent's development stage).
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Threshold/top-k similarity retrieval. The proposed retrieval function returns the subset C_q = R(q,L) = {c_i in L | sim(q,P_i) >= tau}, i.e., a similarity-threshold (tau) selection rather than a fixed-completeness-set or precision-driven variable-size objective. As a review it does not define a completeness metric; surveyed systems mostly use top-k / nearest-neighbor case retrieval.
cbr_cycle_coverage: [Retrieve, Reuse, Revise, Retain] -- all four. The paper explicitly defines and models the full Aamodt & Plaza 4R cycle: Retrieve (case retrieval, Eqs. 2-4), Reuse/Revise (solution adaptation A = A_compose o A_transform o A_select, Eqs. 5-6, 10-12), and Retain (case learning/retention via utility-thresholded library update, Eqs. 7-8). It frames itself entirely around this cycle.
explicit_cbr_grounding: True. The work explicitly frames itself as Case-Based Reasoning and grounds in the canonical CBR literature -- it cites Aamodt & Plaza (1994) for the 4R cycle and lazy learning, Kolodner (1992) for human expert reasoning, plus Craw & Aamodt (2018) and CBR knowledge-container theory. The entire paper is about integrating classic CBR into LLM agents.
retrieval_unit: Case (a structured problem-solution tuple). Formally a case c = (P, S, O, M): P = problem space (features p_1..p_n), S = solution space (actions s_1..s_m), O = outcome space (success metrics o_1..o_k), M = metadata (temporal markers, environmental conditions, provenance). Surveyed instantiations include problem-solution pairs (NL task -> Python code), expert insight cases, and precedent legal/medical cases.
index_source: Growing case library L = {c_1,...,c_l}, constructed both offline (seeded from expert/historical cases, e.g., DS-Agent development stage) and online/test-time-induced via the Retain phase that appends successful new problem-solution episodes. HYBRID: an initial offline case base that grows during deployment.
index_structure_topology: Hierarchical + hybrid index. Each case is indexed with BOTH a dense semantic embedding E_i (from the foundation LLM's latent space) AND sparse feature-based indices I_i capturing domain-specific attributes (Algorithm 1). The library is then organized via a hierarchical structure (OrganizeHierarchy) enabling coarse-to-fine search; a structural-similarity retrieval channel (R_structural) also matches problem-structure / solution-pattern topology.
retriever_type: Hybrid. The proposed hybrid retrieval combines three channels: R_semantic (dense embedding/cosine similarity in the LLM latent space, Eq. 4), R_feature (explicit feature matching), and R_structural (problem-structure / solution-pattern matching), fused by weights lambda_1, lambda_2, lambda_3 (Eq. 9). It is therefore a dense+feature+structural hybrid retriever rather than a single BM25/dense/learned retriever.
retriever_learning_signal: None / off-the-shelf similarity (with fixed/heuristic weights). The retrieval similarity is a weighted sum sim(q,P_i) = sum_j w_j * sim_j(q_j,p_ij) with feature weights w_j and channel weights lambda_1..3 that are specified as parameters/coefficients rather than learned via a described training objective; the semantic channel uses off-the-shelf foundation-model embeddings (cosine similarity). The review does not train a retriever or use contrastive / LM-feedback / RL retrieval signals; weight tuning is left unspecified. [uncertain] whether the weights are intended to be learned.
query_construction: Raw query problem q is matched against the problem component P_i of stored cases; query/key formed from the current problem features (problem-space representation). In the GDA extension, queries are also keyed on (state, goal) for the Plan Case Base and on detected discrepancies/mismatches m for the Mismatch Case Base. No synthetic-query expansion is prescribed.
query_granularity: Both task-level and step/state-level. Base CBR retrieval is task-level (retrieve cases for the query problem q at problem-solving time). The CBR-GDA extension adds step/state-level retrieval: Retrieve_PCB: S x G -> S x P (plan cases keyed on state+goal) and Retrieve_MCB: M -> G (goal cases keyed on discrepancy), invoked during execution monitoring -- a two-level scheme.
when_to_retrieve: One-shot at problem-solving time for the core CBR cycle (retrieve relevant cases for query q, then adapt). In the CBR-GDA cognitive extension retrieval becomes active/iterative: triggered during execution by discrepancy detection (mismatch m between expected and actual state) to retrieve new goals (online monitoring loop).
retrieval_trigger_signal: For core CBR: fixed/once-per-query (retrieve when a new problem q arrives, gated by similarity threshold tau). For CBR-GDA: discrepancy-triggered -- a detected mismatch m = Discrepancy(s_c, e_c, s_actual) between expected and actual states triggers retrieval from the Mismatch Case Base to formulate a new goal (agent-/event-initiated, uncertainty/expectation-violation signal).
reranking: Not explicitly framed as a separate cross-encoder reranking stage. The closest mechanisms are the weighted fusion of the three retrieval channels (lambda_1 R_semantic U lambda_2 R_feature U lambda_3 R_structural, Eq. 9) and the meta-cognitive adaptation-strategy selector; the review does not specify a dedicated reranker. [uncertain] (no explicit rerank stage described).
retrieved_context_refinement: Selection/transformation as part of adaptation rather than a separate refinement pipeline: A_select identifies the most relevant components from retrieved solutions, A_transform modifies them to target constraints, A_compose integrates them (Eq. 6). A meta-cognitive process selects the adaptation approach based on problem characteristics and retrieval results. No explicit distractor-filtering or compression module is described.
how_retrieved_used: Case adaptation / reuse (and prompt augmentation). Retrieved cases C_q are passed to the LLM adaptation function s_hat = A(q, C_q) = f_LLM(q, C_q, Theta); the LLM adapts retrieved solutions into a context-appropriate answer via transformational (substitution/deletion/insertion, Eq. 10), compositional (weighted combination of k solutions, Eq. 11), and generative (LLM-synthesized, Eq. 12) adaptation. Retrieved cases also serve as explicit precedent exemplars for explainability and (surveyed) dynamic few-shot prompting.
planning_integration: Retrieve-then-adapt (case-based plan/solution synthesis), extended to per-execution interleaving in the GDA loop. Core: retrieve cases at plan/solve time, then adapt into a solution. Cognitive extension integrates CBR into a Goal-Driven Autonomy controller (discrepancy detection -> explanation -> goal formulation -> goal management), with two case bases (Plan Case Base mapping state+goal->expectations, Mismatch Case Base mapping discrepancy->new goal) consulted during execution monitoring -- i.e., retrieval woven into a plan-monitor-replan loop.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: Per-answer for the core CBR cycle (retrieve-adapt-answer once per problem). In the CBR-GDA extension it becomes per-step / per-monitoring-cycle: retrieval is invoked each time a discrepancy is detected during execution to reformulate goals. The framework also proposes a weighted blend of reasoning pathways f_reasoning(q) = omega_1 f_CBR + omega_2 f_CoT + omega_3 f_parametric (Eq. 13).
retrieved_item_representation: Structured case (problem-solution-outcome-metadata tuple) injected as explicit precedent/exemplar; the solution component S is adapted into the final answer. Surface forms across surveyed systems include raw problem-solution pairs (NL task + executable Python code), expert insight cases, and nearest-neighbor precedent cases presented alongside difference statements for explainability.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Single concrete case / precedent (a problem-solution episode), not a distilled abstract strategy. Cases retain concrete problem features, solution actions, and outcome metrics; CBR is characterized as lazy learning where generalization is delayed until a specific problem is encountered, so retrieved units stay at the concrete-precedent level (with metadata).
adaptation_mechanism: LLM-prompted adaptation (the LLM is the adaptation engine), formalized as A(q,C_q) = A_compose o A_transform o A_select (Eq. 6) with three sub-types: transformational adaptation (substitution/deletion/insertion operations to fit target constraints, Eq. 10), compositional adaptation (weighted combination of components from k retrieved solutions, Eq. 11), and generative adaptation (LLM synthesizes a novel solution conditioned on retrieved cases, s_adapted = f_LLM(q,{S_1..S_k},Theta), Eq. 12). A meta-cognitive process selects the adaptation strategy by problem characteristics and retrieval results; not execution-feedback or RL-reuse-finetuning based.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Similarity-threshold gating (tau) for retrieval selectivity, plus meta-cognitive / self-reflective adaptation-strategy selection and (in GDA) discrepancy detection that flags expectation violations. The proposed cognitive dimensions (self-reflection, introspection) are positioned as a robustness mechanism. No retriever-aware training or distractor-aware SFT is described (it is a conceptual framework).
memory_type: Episodic case-library memory (skill/case base). The agent maintains a case library L of past problem-solution-outcome episodes; the GDA extension adds two specialized case bases (Plan Case Base, Mismatch Case Base). Framed as experiential / episodic knowledge that mirrors human episodic memory.
write_back: True. The Retain phase stores new problem-solution episodes into the case library: L_{t+1} = L_t U {c_new} if U(c_new, L_t) >= delta, else L_t (Eq. 7). The CBR-GDA variant similarly appends to the Plan and Mismatch Case Bases (Eqs. 18-19).
online_growth: True. The case library grows during deployment/test-time as successful new cases are retained (continuous learning / knowledge evolution); this online growth is presented as a core CBR advantage for domain adaptation (accelerated adaptation trajectories, storing previously unseen scenarios for future reuse).
write_back_trigger: Utility-thresholded retention (selective, quality/effectiveness-gated): a new case is added only if its utility U(c_new, L_t) >= delta (Eq. 7), where U = alpha*novelty + beta*effectiveness + gamma*generalizability (Eq. 8). In CBR-GDA, plan/goal cases are retained only if their Quality exceeds thresholds theta_P / theta_M (Eqs. 18-19). Effectively on-success / high-utility retention with novelty and generalizability considered.
failure_experience_usage: Primarily success/high-utility retention. The retention utility weights effectiveness and generalizability and the GDA updates gate on Quality thresholds, biasing storage toward successful episodes; the paper also notes CBR's ability to store edge cases / exceptional situations explicitly for graceful degradation, but it does not formalize a dedicated failure-only corrective-rule store or success-vs-failure contrastive memory. Mostly success-oriented with explicit storage of exceptional cases. [uncertain] (no explicit negative-case contrastive scheme defined).
memory_evolution_update: Append with selective retention (utility/quality-gated append-only growth). The formal model appends qualifying new cases to the library (Eqs. 7, 18-19); it mentions case acquisition and refinement and selective retention for computational efficiency, but does not specify an explicit dedup-merge / delta-update / forget-prune operator for already-stored cases. Append-only with utility gating. [uncertain] (post-write mutation/pruning not formalized).
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No. Case selection is a fixed similarity-threshold retrieval (sim >= tau) with heuristic weights, not a learned/RL-optimized retrieval policy. The GDA controller learns by updating its case bases (storing high-quality plans/goals), but retrieval/case-selection itself is similarity-based, not an M-MDP or RL retrieval policy.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: Mostly single-agent private case memory, but the cognitive/GDA section reviews a multiagent setting: Munoz-Avila et al.'s CB-GDA used in a multiagent gaming domain with two shared case bases. The proposed framework is largely single-agent; multi-agent/shared-memory CBR is discussed via cited work rather than as a central contribution.
benchmarks: N/A as original experiments (the review runs no benchmarks of its own). It cites empirical results from prior CBR-LLM works: automated data science (DS-Agent, Guo et al. 2024), legal question answering (CBR-RAG / CaseGPT, Wiratunga et al. 2024), triage classification (Wilkerson 2024), logical fallacy detection (Sourati et al. 2023), code generation via dynamic few-shot prompting (Dannenhauer et al. 2024), and multiagent gaming GDA (Munoz-Avila et al. 2010).
benchmark_family: N/A as a primary axis (no benchmark suite of its own). The cited evaluations span: tool/code & automated data science (DS-Agent code-generation tasks), domain-specific QA (legal/healthcare QA for CBR-RAG/CaseGPT), classification (triage classification, logical fallacy detection), and decision/planning in games (multiagent gaming GDA). It does not adopt the standard agentic-trajectory benchmark families (Web/Embodied/Tool/Code/Memory/Decision-RL) as an organizing axis.
baselines: N/A as original comparisons (no head-to-head experiments). Its qualitative comparative analysis (Section 7, Table 1) contrasts three reasoning-approach classes: CBR-LLM vs Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning vs vanilla/standard RAG. Cited works compare their CBR systems against zero-shot, static few-shot prompting (Dannenhauer et al.), baseline LLM agents / other SOTA agents (DS-Agent), and rule-based GDA / non-GDA replanning (CB-GDA).
key_metrics: N/A as original measurement. The review enumerates the metrics used across the surveyed evaluations: accuracy, generalizability, user trust, task completion rate, mean rank, best rank, one-pass rate, cost efficiency, and various explainability metrics. It also proposes conceptual metrics: an explainability score E(a) (Eq. 20), an adaptation rate A(a,d) (Eq. 21), compute time / memory cost (Eqs. 22-23), and a composite solution-quality Q(a) (Eq. 24).
headline_result: Cited (not produced by this review): the DS-Agent CBR framework (Guo et al. 2024) achieved a 100% success rate in the development stage and a 99% one-pass rate in the deployment stage with GPT-4, outperforming other state-of-the-art LLM agents while demonstrating cost efficiency. The review uses this and Wilkerson's triage-trust result and Sourati's fallacy-detection accuracy/generalizability gains as evidence for CBR-LLM advantages; its own central contributions are the 4R mathematical model and the CBR vs CoT vs vanilla-RAG comparison (Table 1).
ablations: N/A (the review conducts no experiments and reports no component ablations of its own). Its closest analogue is the qualitative dimension-by-dimension comparison in Table 1 (Knowledge Utilization, Reasoning Transparency, Adaptation Capacity, Domain Specificity, Learning Mechanism, Cognitive Capabilities, Goal Reasoning) attributing distinct strengths to CBR-LLM vs CoT vs vanilla RAG.
evaluation_decoupling: N/A as original measurement. It conceptually separates an intrinsic explainability metric E(a) (Eq. 20) and adaptation-rate A(a,d) (Eq. 21) from end-task solution quality Q(a) (Eq. 24) and from compute/memory cost (Eqs. 22-23), but reports no measured retrieval-vs-task decoupling (Recall@k/nDCG are not used; it is not an empirical study).
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Both are discussed conceptually. Beyond outcome metrics (accuracy, success/one-pass rate, task completion), the review emphasizes process/transparency metrics -- precedent-based reasoning transparency, an explainability score E(a) = (1/n) sum trace(r_i)/complexity(r_i), user-trust scores, and adaptation rate over time -- arguing CBR's explicit precedent traces give superior explainability vs CoT and vanilla RAG. It measures none of these itself.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Discussed qualitatively/formally, not measured. It formalizes total compute time T(a,q) = T_retrieval + T_processing + T_generation (Eq. 22) and memory M(a) = M_model + M_knowledge + M_working (Eq. 23), arguing CBR incurs extra retrieval cost but benefits from reduced processing for well-matched cases and more efficient knowledge management (selective retention) than corpus-based vanilla RAG. The one cited efficiency claim is DS-Agent's reported cost efficiency with GPT-4.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Similarity-threshold selection (tau) determines the retrieved case set C_q rather than a fixed top-k or token budget; adaptation can compose up to k retrieved solutions (compositional adaptation, Eq. 11). No explicit token/prompt budget or fixed-k value is specified (conceptual framework). [uncertain] (no concrete k or token budget given).
survey_scope_and_axes: Organizing axes: (1) theoretical foundations of CBR-augmented LLM agents (formal case definition c=(P,S,O,M), and a mathematical model of Retrieve/Adapt/Retain); (2) architectural components (case representation & indexing, hybrid retrieval, adaptation mechanisms, integration with LLM reasoning); (3) cognitive dimensions (self-reflection, meta-cognition/introspection, curiosity/extrospection, CBR knowledge-container interactions); (4) Goal-Driven Autonomy (GDA) integration with a CBR-GDA mathematical model and learning; and (5) comparative analysis CBR vs CoT vs vanilla RAG across seven dimensions (Table 1). Reference count: 44 entries (Semantic Scholar referenceCount = 44; bibliography numbered to [44]); coverage window classic CBR (1992-1994) through 2024 CBR-LLM work, with the survey itself published April 2025.
benchmark_construction_and_size: N/A (this is a review, not a benchmark; it constructs no dataset). It cites others' results (e.g., DS-Agent's 100% development success / 99% one-pass deployment with GPT-4) as difficulty/quality signals rather than building or sizing any benchmark.
builds_on: Builds on the classic CBR literature -- Aamodt & Plaza (1994) 4R cycle and lazy learning, Kolodner (1992), Craw & Aamodt (2018) cognitive CBR / knowledge containers -- and on Goal-Driven Autonomy (Munoz-Avila et al. 2010; Langley 2012 cognitive systems). It synthesizes recent CBR-LLM systems it reviews: DS-Agent (Guo et al. 2024), CaseGPT and CBR-RAG (Wiratunga et al. 2024), CBR for code generation (Dannenhauer et al. 2024), logical-fallacy CBR-LLM (Sourati et al. 2023), triage CBR (Wilkerson 2024), and cognitive-architecture/LLM work (Sumers et al. 2023).
contrasts_with: Positions CBR-augmented LLM agents explicitly against Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning and standard/vanilla Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): CBR uses experiential, precedent-based, transparent reasoning with high adaptation capacity, explicit domain modeling, case-acquisition learning, and dynamic goal reasoning, whereas CoT relies on parametric knowledge and static step-based reasoning, and vanilla RAG on reference-based corpus retrieval with corpus-expansion learning (Table 1). It also contrasts CBR-GDA with rule-based GDA and non-GDA replanning (cited).
lineage: Surveys group. A 2025 conceptual/theoretical review that maps the canonical CBR 4R cycle (Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain) onto LLM agents with an explicit mathematical model and a CBR vs CoT vs vanilla-RAG comparison; it anchors group D (case-based / experiential-memory agents) by providing the CBR ontology (explicit Aamodt & Plaza grounding, case = (P,S,O,M), growing case library, retain-driven online learning) that distinguishes true case-based reasoning from plain retrieval-augmentation, complementing method papers such as DS-Agent and CBR-RAG.
